summary: This informational note describes issues raised by the deployment of Internationalized Domain Names, both at registration time and in use within the DNS. It recommends that the IETF update the IDN-related RFCs, proposes a framework for doing so, and suggests investigating changes to IDNA and its tables.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4690 reviews problems that appeared as domain names began using characters beyond ASCII. It recommends further work on character rules, Unicode updates, and registry policies, but defines no new protocol.

questions: what are confusable characters in domain names
subtitle: The IAB reviews internationalized domain-name problems and recommends areas for further work

tldr.problem: Internationalized domain names raised issues with character matching, look-alike names, registry rules, and changes to Unicode.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB reviews these issues and recommends that the IETF and registries consider narrower character lists, future Unicode updates, and dispute policies.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4690 gives advice and a framework for further investigation. It does not change the IDNA protocol.

today: RFC 4690 is an Informational IAB document published in September 2006. Its recommendations are advice for further work, not protocol changes; the supplied metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: How Internationalized Names Fit DNS
sections.content:
Internationalized domain names are DNS names that allow a wider range of characters than traditional hostnames. The IAB says they must still meet the DNS requirements for stable and predictable references.

DNS lookups require exact matches, and every server must apply the same matching rules. The DNS does not provide searches or near matches when a name differs from a registered label.
sections.plainLanguage: A domain name can use characters from more writing systems, but DNS still looks for an exact name. It does not suggest close matches.

sections.title: The IDNA Standards and Unicode
sections.content:
The IDNA system described here uses several related standards. Stringprep defines text preparation, Nameprep applies it to domain names, IDNA defines how applications use the prepared names, and Punycode encodes Unicode text with hostname-compatible characters.

The RFC says these standards depend on Unicode Version 3.2. At the time, there was no established process for moving IDNA to newer Unicode versions.
sections.plainLanguage: Several standards prepare and encode an internationalized name before DNS can use it. RFC 4690 says those rules were tied to Unicode Version 3.2.

sections.title: Matching, Scripts, and Look-Alike Characters
sections.content:
Characters that people treat as equivalent in one language may have different Unicode values or meanings in another. A language may also use more than one script, while some characters from different scripts can look alike on a screen.

These differences can cause names to fail to match or can lead users to the wrong domain. The RFC says algorithms cannot remove every such risk; protocol rules, registry policies, and user-interface design each have a role.
sections.plainLanguage: Two domain names can look alike but refer to different places. A character rule that works for one language may be confusing in another.

sections.title: Updating Unicode Without Breaking Names
sections.content:
Changes to Unicode or its normalization rules can change how a domain-name string is processed. If implementations adopt those changes differently, the same name may behave differently across systems.

The IAB describes a difficult balance: keeping IDNA fixed excludes newer characters, while an unsafe update could make existing names invalid or ambiguous. It recommends investigating a way to support later Unicode versions while preserving stable names.
sections.plainLanguage: Changing text rules can change how an existing domain name is read. Updates need to support new characters without making old names unreliable.

sections.title: Recommendations for the IETF and Registries
sections.content:
The IAB recommends reviewing the IDNA standards and how they use Unicode. It favors investigating an inclusion-based character list, which names allowed characters, and considering whether to allow only the characters needed for language and number labels.

For registries, the RFC recommends defining allowed characters and developing dispute-resolution policies together. It also notes that DNS changes cannot provide approximate matching or solve every problem with names shown to users.
sections.plainLanguage: The IAB advises standards groups and registries to state clearly which characters are allowed. It also recommends ways to handle disputes about names that may confuse users.
